title: How to know God's will?
summary: How to make decisions and discern God's guidance - without the magic of "signs" and without the paralysis of fear. About trust, a renewed mind, the role of the Word, prayer, circumstances, and community, and about how a readiness to obey opens up knowledge of God's will.

sections.heading: Trust the Guide before you know the way

items.comment: "Trust in the Lord with all your heart... and He will make your paths straight." The starting point is not "to know the plan," but "to trust the Person." Guidance is a promise for those who trust, not only for those who analyze.

questions.text: What do you look for more when you ask about God's will: a ready answer, or trust in God amid uncertainty? How do these differ?

items.comment: "I will instruct you and show you the way... I will counsel you, my eye upon you." God Himself declares His readiness to guide. Discerning His will is not extracting secrets, but a relationship with a Counselor who wants to show the way.

questions.text: What changes in seeking a decision when you realize that God wants to guide you more than you want to be guided?

items.comment: "Commit your way to the Lord and trust Him, and He will act." The order: first commitment and trust, then God's action. I do not have to "force" a solution - I am to commit it.

questions.text: Which decision is hardest for you to "commit" to God, because you would rather keep control? What holds you back from doing so?

items.comment: "I know the plans I have for you... plans for peace." God's guidance flows from His good intentions toward me - seeking Him "with all your heart" is part of the promise of finding Him.

questions.text: How are your decisions affected by whether you assume God's intentions toward you are "good," or rather "tricky"?

items.comment: "Be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may discern what the will of God is." Discernment is not a technique or a lottery - it is the fruit of a transformed way of thinking. First the heart and mind are shaped, then we see more clearly.

questions.text: What shapes your way of thinking more today - "this world" or God's renewing work? How can you tell?

items.label: "the renewing of the mind" / ἀνακαίνωσις τοῦ νοός (anakainōsis tou noos) (Rom 12:2)
items.content: Paul connects *anakainōsis* ("renewal, thorough transformation") with *nous* ("mind, way of thinking, mentality"). Here discerning the will of God ("so that you may discern") is the result of a transformed mind, and not a separate technique or a "sign from heaven." The verb "be transformed" (Greek *metamorphousthe*, passive/reflexive, present tense) points to a continual process, carried out by God, and not a one-time act. The practical conclusion: the ability to discern well grows along with how God transforms our values and desires - it is maturing, not a trick.

questions.text: If discernment is the result of a transformed mind, then where should you invest in order to discern God's will better - in "looking for signs" or in the transformation of your thinking?

items.label: "so that you may discern": δοκιμάζω (dokimazō) as discernment through testing (Rom 12:2)
items.content: The verb translated "so that you may discern / test" is the Greek *dokimazō* - a word from the language of assaying: "to examine, to test (like metal in fire), to approve after examination." So discerning the will of God is not a passive waiting for a flash of insight, but an active "testing," in the light of Scripture and a renewed mind, of what is good, pleasing, and perfect. This is an active verb: God's will is tested and confirmed, not drawn by lot. From the same root comes *dokimos* ("tested, proven").

questions.text: What would "testing" the decision you are weighing look like in the light of Scripture, instead of waiting for one unusual "sign"?

items.comment: Right before speaking about discernment, Paul appeals: "offer your bodies as a living sacrifice." Knowing God's will begins with offering yourself - it is hard to hear a direction when you stipulate in advance where you do not want to go.

questions.text: In the question about God's will, is there any area "ruled out in advance" ("anything but that")? How does that affect your hearing of God?

items.comment: "Solid food is for the mature, who by practice have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil." Discernment is a skill that grows through practice - you mature into it, you do not receive it all at once.

questions.text: In which decisions did you, over time, begin to "sense" God's way better? What trained that sense?

items.comment: "Do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is." Knowing God's will is possible and commended - it is not an unreachable secret, but something we are to pursue actively, with a mind enlightened by God.

questions.text: Do you treat God's will as something that can be known, or as a riddle you will not guess anyway? How does that attitude affect your decisions?

sections.heading: Readiness to obey opens up knowledge

items.comment: "If anyone wants to do His will, he will know whether the teaching is from God." Jesus reverses our order: we usually want to know first, then decide whether we will obey. He says: readiness to obey opens our eyes to the truth.

questions.text: What would change if you first told God "I will do what You show me," and only then asked Him to show you?

items.label: John 7:17: the priority of the will to obey before knowing
items.content: In John 7:17 Jesus formulates a principle of knowing that is relational and moral, not purely intellectual: knowing the truth about His teaching depends on a prior readiness ("if anyone wants to do His will"). This reverses the common assumption that you must first have full certainty, and only then is it worth obeying. In the context of discerning God's will this means that a readiness to obey that is not settled in advance is not an obstacle to knowing - it is its condition. Often we do not see the next step not for lack of information, but for lack of consent to what we already know.

questions.text: In your current decision, do you lack information, or rather consent to what deep down you already sense God is showing you?

items.comment: "Not my will, but Yours be done." In Gethsemane Jesus prays for discernment with an open heart - He honestly speaks of His desire, yet submits it to the Father's will. This is the pattern for praying for guidance.

questions.text: Can you tell God honestly what you desire, and at the same time say "may Your will be done"? What is difficult about that?

items.label: "will" in Gethsemane: thelēma and the surrender of desire (Luke 22:42)
items.content: In Jesus' prayer the same word "will" (Greek *thelēma*) appears, applied first to Him and then to the Father: "not my will, but Yours." Discernment here does not consist in suppressing one's own desires or pretending they are not there - Jesus names them plainly - but in consciously subordinating them to the Father's will. This is the pattern of healthy discernment: honesty about one's own wishes plus a real readiness for God to decide otherwise. Prayer for guidance is not a technique for forcing an answer, but an act of trust.

items.comment: "He guides the humble in what is right and teaches them His way." The condition for guidance is humility - a readiness to be taught and to change one's mind. Pride, which already "knows best," is hard to lead.

questions.text: Where in your current decision do you need more humility - a readiness for God to lead you differently than you assumed?

items.comment: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God... and it will be given to him." The first move in discernment is simple: ask. God "gives generously and without reproach" - you can simply ask for wisdom.

questions.text: In your decisions, do you actually ask God for wisdom first, or do you rather analyze on your own first and ask God last?

items.label: "gives generously and without reproach": haplōs (Jas 1:5)
items.content: James encourages us to ask for wisdom from a God who gives to "all" (Greek *haplōs* - "simply, generously, without a divided heart, without hidden reservations"). The image is the opposite of a stingy giver who later reproaches; God does not grant wisdom like a reward for guessing a secret "sign," but generously answers the request of faith. "Wisdom" (Greek *sophia*) in this context is the practical skill of living and deciding well, not secret knowledge of the future. That is why the first and simplest tool of discernment remains prayer for wisdom, not fortune-telling practices.

questions.text: Do you ask God for "wisdom" to make a decision, or rather for the "future to be revealed"? How do these two requests differ?

sections.heading: Tools of guidance: the Word, prayer, circumstances, community

items.comment: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path." The first and sure source of guidance is Scripture. It does not light up the whole road at once, but the "next step" - it gives principles and direction, not a fortune.

questions.text: How concretely do you use the Word when making decisions? Do you look in it for principles and direction, or rather for a "sign on demand"?

items.label: "a lamp to my feet": the image of an oil lamp (Ps 119:105)
items.content: The Hebrew word rendered "lamp" (Hebrew *ner*) means a small clay oil lamp that lit up only the nearest few steps in front of someone walking at night. The image is deliberate: the Word usually does not show the whole road at once or the distant future, but lights up enough for the "next step." This corrects the expectation that Scripture will provide a ready-made script for one's whole life; rather, it gives direction, principles, and light for the current decision. The rest of the road is revealed as we walk in obedience.

questions.text: Do you expect the Word to be a "map of the whole road," or do you accept light only for the next step? How does this change your decisions?

items.label: "let the peace of Christ rule": βραβεύω (brabeuō) (Col 3:15)
items.content: In Col 3:15 Paul writes that the peace of Christ should "rule" in our hearts (Greek *brabeuō*) - a verb from the world of athletic contests, meaning "to act as umpire/arbiter, to award the prize, to decide the contest." So peace acts as an inner arbiter that helps us judge between options. Note: this is not an autonomous "sign" or a feeling above Scripture - it is the peace of *Christ*, in the body that is the Church, in agreement with the Word. Peace can be a confirmation or a warning, but always one subordinate to Scripture, never above it.

questions.text: Do you verify the "peace" you feel about a decision by the Word and the counsel of community, or do you treat the feeling itself as the final verdict?

items.comment: "In everything... let your requests be made known to God, and the peace of God... will guard your hearts." Prayer about a decision often brings not so much an audible answer as a "peace" that guards the heart - an inner confirmation or unease about a direction.

questions.text: In your decisions, do you pay attention to the "peace" or "unease" after prayer? How do you tell God's peace from mere relief that you have finally decided?

items.comment: "Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed." God also guides through wise people. Community and trusted advisers protect us from self-deception and blind spots.

questions.text: Whom do you ask for advice on important decisions? Do you look for advisers who will "applaud" you, or ones who will tell you the truth?

items.label: "many advisers": a recurring principle in Proverbs (Prov 11:14; 15:22; 24:6)
items.content: The theme of "safety in many advisers" recurs several times in Proverbs (Prov 11:14; 15:22; 24:6), which underscores its weight as a lasting principle of wisdom rather than a one-off remark. The Hebrew background is military and administrative language: a prudent ruler does not plan a battle alone. Transferred to discerning God's will, this means that the counsel of a mature community is an ordinary, God-given tool of guidance - it guards against blind spots and self-deception. At the same time, "many" implies a diversity of voices, not only those that will confirm a decision already made.

questions.text: Are you building around yourself a "multitude" of different wise advisers, or rather one circle that usually thinks the way you do?

items.comment: "The heart of a person plans his way, but the Lord directs his steps." We are to plan - and at the same time remember that the final directing belongs to God. Circumstances that "open and close doors" can be part of that directing (cf. Acts 16:6-10).

questions.text: How do you keep the balance between "planning your way" (planning) and "letting God direct your steps" (flexibility)? Which side prevails in you?

items.label: "signs" and casting lots, and the ban on divination (Deut 18:9-14; cf. Gideon's fleece, Judg 6)
items.content: Deut 18:9-14 firmly forbids divination, fortune-telling by times, sorcery, and "consulting the dead" - pagan practices that try to force hidden knowledge apart from God. This warns against treating random "signs," casting lots, or a pendulum as a way of discerning God's will; the core of the problem is an attempt to control the future instead of trusting the God revealed in the Word. Gideon's "fleece" (Judg 6:36-40) is sometimes cited as a method, but the Bible describes it as an exceptional, cautious gesture of weak faith in response to a promise already given - not a model to imitate. In the sola scriptura view, guidance rests on Scripture, prayer, wisdom, counsel, providence, and peace, not on quasi-magical "tests."

questions.text: Do you sometimes look for a "sign on demand" instead of asking what Scripture and wisdom already say? Where does this temptation come from?

items.comment: "Your ears will hear a word... This is the way, walk in it!" The promise of guidance is addressed to those who are walking - God more often corrects the course "along the way" than shows the whole map at the start. You have to start walking.

questions.text: Do you wait for the "whole map" before you set out? What would it mean to take a wise first step and let God correct you along the way?

items.comment: "Make me know the way I should go... teach me to do Your will, for You are my God; let Your good Spirit lead me." This pattern of praying for guidance joins a request to know the way with a request for the Spirit Himself as Guide.

questions.text: What would your own prayer for guidance look like if you asked not only for an "answer," but for the Spirit Himself as Guide?

items.label: "the will of God": distinguishing what is revealed from what is specific
items.content: Scripture speaks of God's will on two levels. (1) The revealed will - expressed directly in the Word, concerning character and conduct (e.g., 1 Thess 4:3 "this is the will of God, your sanctification"; 1 Thess 5:18 "give thanks"); here there is no need to "discern," only to obey. (2) The specific/situational will - choices the Bible does not settle directly (work, place, relationships); here wisdom operates, shaped by the Word, prayer, peace, circumstances, and community, within the freedom God gives His mature children. Confusing the levels produces two errors: looking for a "magic sign" where God has given freedom and wisdom, or "discerning" whether to obey what has already been clearly revealed. In the spirit of sola scriptura, the point of reference always remains Scripture; prayer, circumstances, and the counsel of community are subordinate to it, never above it.

questions.text: Which of the two spheres concerns your current decision - what God has already clearly revealed, or what He has left to your wisdom? How does this change the way you seek an answer?

application.text: Discerning God's will is not guessing hidden signs or being paralyzed by the fear of "making a mistake." It is, above all, trusting the God who wants to guide, and letting Him transform our way of thinking. When we agree in advance to obey (John 7:17), knowing becomes easier. God guides not by magic, but through the Word (direction and principles), prayer (peace that guards the heart), wise circumstances, and a trusted community - and where He has left freedom, He invites us to decide wisely as His mature children and to set out on the way, trusting that He will correct the course.
application.challenge: Take one decision you are now weighing, and run it through the "five channels" of guidance: (1) The Word - what biblical principles apply to it? (2) Prayer - ask for wisdom (Jas 1:5) and say honestly, "not my will, but Yours" (Luke 22:42); notice peace or unease. (3) Circumstances - what "doors" is God opening or closing? (4) Community - ask 1-2 trusted, wise people (Prov 15:22). (5) Obedience - declare in advance your readiness to do what you discern (John 7:17). Then take a wise first step, instead of waiting for the "whole map" (Isa 30:21).
